title: Job seekers trafficked into Cambodia scam compounds: what we know
excerpt: Cambodia deported more than 3,300 Bangladeshis in three years. Rights groups say about 1,800 more are stranded and want to come home.
content:
Bangladeshi job seekers promised office work in Cambodia are being sold into online scam compounds, where their passports and phones are taken and they are forced to defraud people online, according to returnees, BRAC and a survivors’ group. The Daily Star has reported on the issue repeatedly, most recently on 7 November.

The numbers

  • Cambodia’s interior ministry says it deported 3,364 Bangladeshis between 1 September 2023 and 13 September 2026, 852 of them linked to online scams.
  • 15,963 Bangladeshis received government clearance to work in Cambodia between January 2025 and September 2026, according to BMET data cited by BRAC.
  • BRAC had helped 583 people return from Cambodia by June 2026, including 109 rescued from scam compounds.
  • The Bangladesh mission in Thailand has received help requests from 1,796 people in Cambodia. About 300 to 400 had returned by late October.

How people are recruited

Recruiters advertise computer operator, data entry and customer service jobs paying Tk 50,000 to over Tk 1 lakh a month, BRAC says. Victims pay Tk 2 lakh to Tk 7 lakh in fees. Many travel legally, with passports, visas and government clearance, which shows the problem is not only irregular migration. One returnee told The Daily Star he paid Tk 7.70 lakh for a data entry job and was sold to a compound for about US$2,000, where he was given electric shocks when he missed targets.

Shariful Hasan, associate director of BRAC’s Migration Programme, has described the practice as “cyber slavery”.

What survivors are asking for

On 18 October, the Anirban Survivor Voice Foundation wrote to the expatriates’ welfare minister and senior officials saying more than 1,800 Bangladeshis were stranded in Cambodia, bdnews24.com Bangla reported. It asked for repatriation before Cambodia’s overstay fine waiver ran out on 31 October, prosecution of recruiters, treatment of victims as victims rather than criminals, and medical, mental health and legal support on return. These figures come from the foundation; the government had not responded in that report.

Why it matters

Migration NGOs, legal aid groups and organisations running pre-departure orientation can warn job seekers about these offers, especially in districts with high migration. Returnees need trauma care, legal help and support to repay debts, and few services exist for them.

What to watch

Whether the government arranges repatriation flights, acts against the recruiting agencies involved, and tightens clearance for jobs in Cambodia.
